phase and κ-carbide fraction decreased and γ phase fraction increased, and ultimate elongation increased, while ultimate strength and yield strength had a decreasing trend. The γ phase fraction in the specimen dominated the ultimate elongation, and the κ-carbide strengthened the specimen and weakened ductility. As the annealing temperature rose from 900 °C to 1200 °C, the phase fraction change was small but the grain size increased greatly. The rapid growth of the grains was the main reason why ultimate tensile strength and ultimate elongation decreased with the increase of annealing temperature over 900 °C. The steel designed here possessed a density of 6.80 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, which is about 13% lower than pure iron.

The demand for increasing the efficiency of fuel and decreasing the emission of exhaust gas has become more and more prominent in automotive industry, as considered from both environment and energy source aspects. Reducing the weight of automobiles is a good idea for the demand and much effort has been done to improve the strength and ductility of steels used for automotive industry, which will reduce the weight of automobiles by reducing the necessary thickness of steels [1,2]. Twinning induced plasticity (TWIP) steel and transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) steel are representative high-strength steels, containing a high amount of Mn [3–12]. Adding or increasing the Al content in the steel will decrease the density of the steel as Al has a low density. Since low-density high-strength steels can reduce the weight of automobiles more efficiently, Fe–Mn–Al–C steel with a high amount of Al has attracted much attention [1,13,14].

The phases in Fe–Mn–Al–C steels mainly include ferrite, austenite, and κ-carbide [1,15–20]. The κ-carbide has a perovskite structure, and can form by decomposition of austenite or the ordering process in austenite [2,21,22]. The structure of κ-carbide is based on the face-centered cubic crystal lattice, with Fe or Mn atoms occupying the face-centered positions, Al atoms occupying the cornered positions and C atoms occupying the body-centered positions. The space group of κ-carbide is Pm3m. In addition, B2 and
ordered phases may also appear in the steel [23]. The space groups of B2 phase and

phase are Pm3m and Fm3m, respectively. B2 phase is based on body centered cubic crystal lattice, Fe or Mn atoms occupying cornered positions, and Al atoms occupying centered positions (the positions of Fe or Mn atoms and the positions of Al atoms are equivalent). For the structure of

phase, it can be regarded as that every other position occupied by Al atom in the B2 structure is replaced by Fe or Mn atom. Sketches of the structures of the ordered phases are given by Ha et al. [23]. Mn and C are austenitic stabilizing elements, while Al is a strong ferrite forming element. Ferrite is inevitable in the steel with a high Al concentration [1]. Temperature may largely affect the microstructure of the steel, and then affect the mechanical properties. Frommeyer et al. studied the steel Fe–26/ 28Mn–10/12Al–1.0/1.2C composed of ferrite, austenite and nano-sized κ-carbide dispersed in the austenite, whose enhanced ductility is attributed to the homogeneous shear band formation, and the existence of nano-sized κ-carbide coherent to the austenitic matrix [24]. In the steel Fe–27Mn–12Al–0.8C studied by Park, there are B2 and

ordered phases in ferrite and κ-carbide in austenite, which are considered to contribute to the high work hardening rate by acting as obstacles for dislocation glide [23]. Another steel with degraded Mn, Al and C contents, Fe–20Mn–9Al–0.6C, studied by Park et al. reveals no or undetectable ordered phase in the duplex microstructure and has lower ultimate strength than Fe–27Mn–12Al–0.8C [23,25]. Ding et al. investigated steels Fe–12Mn–8Al–0.8C and Fe–18Mn–10Al–(0.8–1.2)C, which contain Mn content less than 20 wt.% and Al content more than 8 wt.%, and results show that, the ductility of Fe–18Mn–10Al–0.8C which composed of ferrite and austenite is less than that of Fe–18Mn–10Al–1.2C which composed of austenite and dispersed κ-carbide when temperature is higher than

while Fe–12Mn–8Al–0.8C composed of ferrite, austenite and dispersed κ-carbide exhibits similar ultimate strength and ductility with Fe–18Mn–10Al–0.8C [26,27]. The ductility of the fully austenitic steels usually seems to be superior to that of the steels containing ferrite, and the nano-size κ-carbide dispersed in the austenite may promote the ductility [17,28–30].

Although lots of investigations have been done on the microstructure and mechanical properties of low-density high-strength Fe–Mn– Al–C steels, most of them are focused on the steels containing Mn content near or more than 20 wt.%, and the microstructure and mechanical properties of the steels containing a high Al and a relative low Mn and C contents should be studied. Thus, a low-density steel Fe–10Mn–10Al– 0.7C is designed and the microstructure and tensile properties after annealed at various temperatures of the steel are investigated in the present study.

The constituent phases were identified at first by the X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku, D/Max-RB) analysis with a Cu target operated at 40 kV and 150 mA. Microstructures were examined by optical microscope (OM, Zeiss AxioCam MRc5), field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM, FEI Quanta 450) operated at an acceleration voltage of 20 kV and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEOL 2100) operated at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV. The SEM is equipped with an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), which can be used to examine the chemical composition of the points or areas of interest. The specimens for OM and SEM observations were mechanically polished and then etching by 8% Nital. After solidification, the phase fraction of ferrite will decrease and that of austenite will increase with the decrease of temperature until the temperature reaches around

Apparently, a part of body-centered cubic (BCC) ferrite will always exist without transforming to facecentered (FCC) austenite, and this part of ferrite is often referred to as δ-ferrite [34,35]. The δ-ferrite usually exhibits coarse grains in the microstructure [13,34]. In the present study, δ-ferrite is not separately treated with α-ferrite. There is difference in the phase fractions and the eutectoid temperature for κ-carbide between the result calculated by Thermo-Calc and that measured from the steel, which will discussed later. The differences may come from that, the steel in the study is not in equilibrium state, and that the calculated fractions are based on the atomic fraction, while the measured fraction from XRD results is based on the volume fraction [34].
The microstructure of hot rolled specimen (marked as

is shown in Fig. 3. Fig. 3(a) and (b) is OM micrographs of RD–ND (rolling direction–normal direction) plane, RD–TD (rolling direction–transverse direction) plane, respectively. As shown in Fig. 3(a), typical banded structure is presented, and coarse ferrite formed during the early stage of solidification steel is obviously observed. It is easy to see that the microstructure is very inhomogeneous in Fig. 3(b), and, large α phase area (the continuous area that mainly contains α phase, while there are also some γ phase or κ-carbide dispersed) and γ phase area (the continuous area that mainly contains γ phase, while there are also some α phase or κ-carbide dispersed) can be used to describe the microstructure. SEM micrograph in Fig. 3(c) clearly shows the κ-carbide along ferrite/austenite (α/γ) and ferrite/ferrite
boundaries. EDS is used to confirm the α phase, γ phase, and κ-carbide, since α phase is Al-rich, γ phase is Mn-rich and C-rich, while κ-carbide is Mn-rich and Al-rich [15,18,34].

paragraph_content.content: XRD results of hot rolled and annealed specimens are shown in Fig. 4. The peaks of κ-carbide are seen in specimen annealed at
and no obvious peaks of γ phase can be seen in the specimen annealed at

. In the hot rolled specimen, peaks of κ- carbide are not seen, probably due to the low volume fraction of κ- carbide, or the coherency of κ-carbide and α matrix [36]. Lattice parameters can be calculated from the XRD profiles, and results show that the lattice parameter of α phase changes in the range 2.89–2.91 Å, the lattice parameter of γ phase changes in the range 3.65–3.67 Å, and the lattice parameter of κ-carbide changes in the range 3.76–3.79 Å. The lattices of α phase and γ phase have been slightly expanded by Mn, Al and C atoms, and being larger than the lattices of α phase and γ phase in Fe–3.5Mn–5.8Al–0.35C, respectively [34]. It is said that the lattice of κ-carbide is mainly governed by the interstitial element, C, while the increment of Al would also bring expansion to the κ lattice and because Mn has a larger atomic radius than Fe, the substitute of Fe by Mn in κ- carbide would also cause slight expansion in the κ-carbide lattice [15, 34]. The lattice expansion of α phase and γ phase, which are the main phase constituents in the steel, will contribute to the low density of the steel.

The microstructures of the steel after annealing for 1 h at the temperature range 700 °C to

in the present study are basically composed of ferrite (α), austenite (γ) and κ-carbide, and the banded structure still exists after the annealing. The morphology, distribution and volume fraction of the α phase, γ phase and κ-carbide affect the tensile properties of the steel. The evolution of the microstructure and its effect on the tensile properties are discussed here.

The relatively good tensile properties of the present steel can be obtained after annealing at

for 1 h, when the ultimate strength, yield strength, ultimate elongation, and the product of strength of strength and ductility, are 855 MPa, 651 MPa, 36.6%, and 31 GPa%, respectively. Tensile properties of the present steel, together with tensile properties of several Fe–Mn–Al–C steels investigated by other researchers [25–27,50] are shown in Table 2. It should be noted that the κ-carbide in the Fe–18Mn–10Al–1.2C, Fe–18Mn–10Al-–0.8C and Fe– 12Mn–8.0Al-0.8C is dispersed in the austenite matrix, which usually promotes planar glide during deformation and contributes to strength. The ultimate strength and ultimate elongation of the present steel are not as good as the other listed steels. In Table 2, it can be easily noticed that the ultimate elongations of the steels containing α phase (Fe– 20Mn–9Al–0.6C, Fe–18Mn–10Al–0.8C and Fe–12Mn–8.0Al–0.8C) are lower than those of the steels containing no α phase (Fe–28Mn–10Al– 1.0C and Fe–18Mn–10Al–1.2C). The ultimate elongation is lowest among the steels in Table 2. Considering the highest α phase fraction in the present steel among the steels, the boundary κ-carbide between some large α grains, and the inhomogeneous microstructure, it is understandable why the ultimate elongation of the present steel is lowest among the steels. There is nearly no κ-carbide dispersed in the γ matrix of the present steel, and the ultimate strength of the present steel is lower than that of Fe–18Mn–10Al–0.8C and Fe–12Mn–8.0Al–0.8C. Since Mn content in the present steel is designed to be low, the C content may need to be increased to improve the mechanical properties. According to the comparison between Fe–18Mn–10Al–1.2C and Fe– 18Mn–10Al–0.8C investigated by Ding et al., the loss of strength by the reduction of Mn content may be compensated by addition of C content. In addition, tensile properties of the present steel are affected more easily by heat treatment temperature than Fe–20Mn–9Al–0.6C [25]. Anyhow, the investigation of the tensile properties and microstructure of the present steel, Fe–10Mn–10Al–0.7C, is important for the future designs and investigations of Mn-lean Fe–Mn–Al–C steels.

paragraph_content.content: In the present study, a Mn-lean Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steel with the chemical composition Fe–10Mn–10Al–0.7C (wt.%) is annealed at the temperature range
to 1200 °C for 1 h. The microstructure evolution during annealing and the relationship between tensile properties and microstructure of the annealed specimens are investigated.
(1) The density of the steel is 6.80 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, about 13% lower than that of pure iron. The largest product of strength and ductility, 31 GPa%, is achieved at the annealing temperature of
when the ultimate strength, yield strength, and ultimate elongation are 855 MPa, 651 MPa and 36.6%, respectively.
(2) The phases presented in the annealed steel mainly include ferrite (α), austenite (γ) and κ-carbide (κ). The dissolution temperature of κ-carbide is between 850 °C and 900 °C. When annealed at 700

γ phase transforms to κ-carbide with lamellar morphology and α phase by eutectoid reaction. With the increase of temperature, the γ phase fraction first increases, and reaches largest, about 63% at around
, and then decreases slightly. The boundary κ-carbide formed during quenching exists in all the specimens annealed at the range
Generally, the α grains and γ grains grow up quickly when the annealing temperature is over 900 °C.
(3) The ultimate strength of the annealed specimens has a decreasing trend with the increase of temperature, while the ultimate elongation first increases until anneal temperature reaches 900
and then decreases with the continued increase of temperature. The change of ultimate strength is sharp, so the window for controlling the tensile properties is relatively small.

and 900 °C, the ductility of the specimens is mainly controlled by the fraction of γ phase. Although the κ-carbide can contribute to the strength, microcracks preferred to initiate around κ-carbide, which is detrimental to the tensile properties. At the annealing temperature between

, since the change of phase fractions is very moderate, the grain sizes, instead of phase fraction change, have a significant effect on the tensile properties. The ultimate strength and ultimate elongation both decrease with the increase of grain sizes when increasing the annealing temperature.
